synopsis: Traceability is a bidirectional written chain from safety claims through requirements, scenarios and tests to recorded evidence; the programme should establish this mapping before hardware is available and challenge disconnected work or unsupported claims [f12190, f1001, f727, f9818]. The operational test chain adds functional performance requirements, individual runs, results and safety-case evidence, while the credibility chain adds real-world referents, model credibility, uncertainty and residual-risk decisions [f7105, f10795]. Reproducibility requires detailed run manifests, archived tool and configuration versions, and traceable calibration inputs; missing binary or configuration provenance prevents results from being tied to an exact product state [f7108, f9386, f7043, f5664]. Before prototype arrival, the recommended safety analysis should derive requirements for failure to intervene and incorrect intervention, allocate performance levels, and map each safety requirement to simulation, hardware-in-the-loop or machine testing [f10530, f10542, f11095]. The decisive early demonstration is a single “golden thread” from a real test through a model and virtual result to a residual-risk decision: failure to demonstrate it by the first half of 2027 is an early warning, and simply multiplying scenarios would increase questionable evidence rather than assurance [f10919, f12195, f12196, f10796]. Traceability alone does not establish credibility: simulation traceability remains a validation item omitted from the machine-motion questions, and updates without regression and revalidation could leave 2027 evidence certifying an obsolete configuration [f6608, f11252].
